title: Photography and Hyper-Realism
answer: Synthetic portraiture, lighting rigs, upscaling, product mockups and virtual location scouting.

children.name: Synthetic Portraiture
children.blurb: Synthetic portraiture is the creation of photographic-style likenesses of people who do not exist, or the re-rendering of real people in new poses, lighting, and settings.

children.name: Lighting Rigs and Relighting
children.blurb: Lighting rigs and relighting in AI photography and hyper-realism cover the placement, intensity, color, and shape of virtual light sources in a scene, and the process of changing how an existing image is lit without rebuilding the scene.

children.name: Upscaling and Noise Reduction
children.blurb: Upscaling and noise reduction in photography and hyper-realism covers the processes that increase image resolution and remove grain, sensor noise, or compression artifacts while preserving or enhancing fine detail.

children.name: Product and Fashion Mockups
children.blurb: Product and fashion mockups use AI image generation to create photorealistic previews of clothing, accessories, packaging, and other goods without a physical photo shoot.

children.name: Virtual Location Scouting
children.blurb: Virtual location scouting uses generative image and video models to produce photorealistic previews of potential filming locations before a physical recce.

sections.body: This field is about using image generation models to create or alter photographs that look as if a camera took them. Current work includes generating faces that do not belong to real people, changing the apparent lighting in an existing photo, enlarging low resolution images while adding plausible detail, placing a product into a scene without a physical shoot, and previewing a real location before sending a crew. The models are not just filters, they reconstruct geometry, materials, and light paths from training data. The site tracks 1000 live image generation models, and many of them are used for exactly these tasks. The output is often indistinguishable from a photograph at first glance, which is the point.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The work is uneven. Synthetic portraiture is mature for front facing, well lit faces, but hands, teeth, and consistent identity across multiple images remain hard. Relighting works well on simple scenes but fails on transparent or highly reflective surfaces. Upscaling and noise reduction are reliable for mild cases, yet they can invent texture that was never in the original, which is a real limit for forensic or archival use. Product and fashion mockups are good enough for early concepting but not for final catalog photography when fabric drape and stitching must be exact. Virtual location scouting can produce useful mood boards, but the generated images are not survey data and cannot replace a site visit for measurements or safety. The honest limit is that these tools produce plausible images, not verified reality.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader who wants to understand fake but believable faces should start with Synthetic Portraiture, which explains how identity is constructed and where it breaks. Lighting Rigs and Relighting then shows how the same underlying models can move a light source after the fact, and it pairs naturally with the portraiture page because faces are the most common test subject. Upscaling and Noise Reduction covers the opposite direction, taking a poor or small image and adding detail, which is useful background before reading Product and Fashion Mockups, where a low quality render is often upscaled into a presentable preview. Virtual Location Scouting sits at the end because it combines portraiture, relighting, and upscaling into a single workflow for pre-production. Together the pages move from creating a single convincing subject to altering light and detail, then to commercial mockups and finally to scouting a whole scene.
